newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs vote on Klaus record after dirty campaign.
newsitem.headline: Czechs vote on Klaus record after dirty campaign.

text.p: Czechs will pass judgment on central Europe's last conservative government in Senate elections this weekend after the meanest, dirtiest campaign since the restoration of democracy.
Past Czech election campaigns since the 1989 fall of communism have often been pedestrian or downright dull.

But although the newly-created Senate will have few powers, President Vaclav Havel has been forced to try to restore order to this campaign after it degenerated into a slanging match over allegations of politically-inspired espionage.
At the centre of the row lies the personal hatred of the two main antagonists of Czech politics: Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and the opposition Social Democrat chairman Milos Zeman.

Both are members of the lower house, where most power lies, but both are also eager for their parties to do well. Opinion polls indicate a close race in the first round on Friday and Saturday, followed by a run-off on November 22 and 23.
The espionage row began last Friday when Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux alleged the state intelligence agency BIS had spied on him three years ago and covered up the operation.
Zeman joined in, accusing Klaus and his Civic Democratic Party (ODS) of using the agency to collect compromising information on himself and other top Social Democrats.
On Monday Klaus, already under pressure after losing his lower house majority earlier this year, seemed on the ropes. He was forced to ditch his protege, BIS director Stanislav Devaty.
The junior parties in Klaus's coalition had been trying for at least two years to unseat Devaty, suspecting that the ODS wanted to use the BIS for its own political dirty tricks.

By Tuesday afternoon, Klaus had turned the tables on Zeman. Interior Minister Jan Ruml was dispatched to meet Havel at his country cottage and came away with just what the ODS wanted -- a presidential putdown for the Social Democrat chief.
Havel, a former political prisoner, bristles at any suggestion that the country he led back to democracy is returning to the ways of communism.
"I can only say that I consider (Zeman's) statements to be extremely irresponsible," he said. "It damaged the image and interests of our country and it can trigger unrest in society."

Havel challenged Zeman to back up his claims. "If his statements are proved to be unfounded I think he should at least apologise to all of those affected," he said. "He should clearly say we are living in a democratic state and not in a state which is quietly, secretly becoming a police state."
Havel, who has a strong bipartisan reputation, also rebuked the ODS for believing it had the right to name a new spymaster.
But it was the Zeman putdown which grabbed the headlines. The separate allegations made by Lux, which are backed up by evidence, have been almost forgotten in the hue and cry.

Klaus may have won this skirmish but few politicians if any have emerged from the campaign looking good. Klaus and Zeman, whose personal hatred dates from the communist period, have called each other liars during the campaign.

Klaus, the last conservative premier in a region which has largely re-elected reform communists in recent years, has to share power with Zeman after his coalition fell two seats short of a majority in lower house polls last June.
He has questioned Zeman's claim that the Social Democrats are a Western-style centre-left party which wants nothing to do with reformed communism.
Accusing Zeman of colluding with the little-reformed Communists, he said that the Social Democracts fundamentally questioned the entire post-1989 economic reform process.
Zeman retorted that Klaus has done nothing to tackle widespread corruption and cronyism. As the insults flew, Klaus accused Zeman of spreading "pure, distilled evil and hatred".
